claims.text: The unmodified alloy is prone to cracking and has poor mechanical integrity.
Infiltration or co-sintering with 10–20 vol% Ag will produce a continuous, percolating binder phase.
The Ag binder will occupy grain boundaries and intergranular regions.
A continuous Ag phase will provide ductile mechanical support.
The continuous Ag phase will improve heat transport.
The Ag binder will bridge cracks.
The Ag binder will distribute stress through the composite.
Crack bridging and stress redistribution will increase compressive strength and fracture resistance.
Silver has sufficiently high thermal conductivity to enhance heat transport in this composite.
Silver is non-magnetic under the proposed operating conditions.
Silver will be chemically inert toward the HEA matrix under fabrication and operation.
The non-magnetic and chemically inert character of Ag will minimize interference with the magnetocaloric and barocaloric transitions.
Adding 10–20 vol% Ag will increase compressive strength to greater than 200 MPa.
The Ag composite will have at least five times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing composites.
The Ag composite will approach the thermal conductivity of In-containing composites.
The caloric response under magnetic-field and pressure cycling will remain at 90–100% of the unmodified alloy value.
Ag contents above 20 vol% would dilute the caloric response excessively.

contradictions.description: The predicted strength is >200 MPa, but a result between 150 and 200 MPa would violate that prediction without meeting the stated falsification condition.
The predicted retained caloric response is 90–100%, but a measured value from 80% to below 90% would violate the prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.

Compressive loading is bounded at 200 MPa, which is insufficient to directly demonstrate a claimed compressive strength greater than 200 MPa unless the test is continued beyond the stated loading boundary.
